channel.title: Oleksandr Shepotylo
channel.description: What trade policy actually does at the level of the firm.

item.title: How did the Brexit uncertainty impact services exports of UK firms?
item.description:
Brexit-related uncertainty had a measurable, negative effect on UK firms’ services exports — distinct from, and in some respects larger than, the effect of the tariff and non-tariff barriers that eventually took effect. Using firm-level export data and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we isolate the uncertainty channel from the trade-policy channel by comparing UK firms to a synthetic control built from firms in countries that faced no comparable shock.

Published in: Journal of International Business Policy, 8(1), 80–104

item.title: Shocked by COVID: Exporting along global value chains
item.description:
COVID-19 hit firms embedded in global value chains differently depending on their position in the chain — upstream suppliers and downstream assemblers absorbed the shock through different channels. Using UK firm-level export data spanning the pandemic, we trace how GVC position shaped the size and persistence of the export shock, and how much of the disruption has since reversed.

Working paper: CEP Discussion Papers dp2105

item.title: Impact of TB Epidemic on Worker and Firm Productivity: Regional Perspective from Ukraine
item.description:
Tuberculosis remains a significant regional health burden in Ukraine, with prevalence varying sharply across oblasts. We link regional TB incidence to worker- and firm-level productivity outcomes, asking how much of Ukraine’s regional productivity gap this specific health channel can account for — evidence with direct relevance to postwar health and labour policy.

Working paper: GLO Discussion Paper Series 1360

item.title: Non-tariff measures and productivity of Ukrainian food-processing firms
item.description:
Non-tariff measures imposed by trading partners act as a quality filter on Ukrainian food-processing exporters: firms that clear them see productivity gains, while the compliance costs push less productive firms out of export markets entirely. Using firm-level microdata, we separate this selection effect from the direct within-firm productivity effect of meeting stricter standards — evidence directly relevant to Ukraine’s ongoing agrifood market access negotiations with the EU.

Published in: Journal of Agricultural Economics, 73(1), 234–256

item.title: Non-tariff measures, quality and exporting: evidence from microdata
item.description:
Non-tariff measures are often treated in policy debate as pure trade friction, but firm-level evidence shows they also act as a quality signal: compliance raises the price premium exporters can command in destination markets, partially offsetting the compliance cost. We quantify this trade-off using product-level export microdata.

Published in: European Review of Agricultural Economics, 47(2), 719–751

item.title: Services liberalization and productivity of manufacturing firms
item.description:
Liberalizing services sectors — telecoms, transport, finance — raises the productivity of the manufacturing firms that use those services as inputs, not just the productivity of the liberalized sector itself. Using Ukrainian firm-level panel data, we trace this indirect productivity channel and show it is large enough to matter for the sequencing of liberalization reforms.

Published in: The Economics of Transition, 23(1), 1–44
